2. In the last Presidential Election, the electioneering fever reached its peak in the first part of November, 1981 and in the course of the election Campaign two groups of rival political parties came to a clash in a place called Jogini Hatkhola in the district of Tangail. In that incident one Kallyan Behari Das received dagger blows to which he immediately succumbed. He was a member of the procession brought out by the supporters of the Presidential candidate, Dr. Kamal Hossain, while the other procession was brought out by the supporters of the Presidential candidate, Justice Sattar. On the same day, 9 November, 1981, one Shaukat Raja lodged a First Information Report with the police alleging that his group was attacked by the supporters of the candidate, Justice Sattar and that accused persons dealt dagger blows to Kallyan Behari Das causing his death. The police registered a case and after investigation submitted Final Report. The Sub-Divisional magistrate, Tangail, accepted the Final Report and discharged the accused by an order dated 26 December, 1981. The Informant, Shaukat Raja. challenging the Final Report, submitted a naraji-petition before the Magistrate on 6 January, 1982, but on 3 February, 1982 he withdrew the naraji-petition which was then ordered by the Magistrate to be "filed". But on 3 March 1982, one Khorshed Alam, who was cited as a witness in the First Information Report, filed a fresh complaint before the Magistrate against the same accused persons on the same allegation and this was registered as C.R. Case No. 299(1) 82 under various sections including section 302 of the Penal Code,. The Magistrate examined the complainant on oath, held an enquiry himself, and on the basis of the materials thus obtained took cognizance of the offence of murder and issued warrant of arrest against 17 persons including the two appellants before us under section 302 read with sections 34 and 109 of the Penal Code, by an order dated 10 June, 1982. This proceeding was challenged by an application under section 561A of the Criminal Procedure Code but the learned Judges of the High Court Division by their impugned order dated 24 November, 1982 dismissed the application refusing to quash the proceedings. 

 3. Mr. T. H. Khan, learned Advocate for the appellants, contends that the appellants were, in fact, discharged twice before on the same allegation and now they have faced the same allegation for the third time; but as there is no fresh evidence brought against them it is not at all open to the learned Magistrate to entertain the complaint, which according to him is the third complaint. The learned Advocate argues that the Naraji-petition dated 6 January 1982 tiled by the Informant Shaukat Raja is the second-complaint as it was filed after acceptance of the Final-report which is the equivalent of a complaint petition. He further argues that if there is no restriction to, or qualification of, the Magistrate's power to entertain fresh complaints on the same allegations, complaints may continue to be filed one after another in perpetuity and there will be no finality of prosecution The learned Advocate contends that 'exceptional circumstances' must exist to justify entertainment of a second complaint after dismissal of the previous one, e.g. where the previous order of dismissal was manifestly illegal or unjust, or it caused miscarriage of justice or it was passed on incomplete record or on misunderstanding of the nature of the complaint or where new facts, which could not, with reasonable diligence, have been brought on record in the previous proceeding. None of these requirements, the learned Advocate contends, are found fulfilled in the instant case. in the absence of any exceptional ground the entertainment of the fresh complaint is a mere abuse of the process of the Court, the learned Advocate further contends, and in support of this contention he has placed reliance upon a decision of the Indian Supreme Court in the case of Pramatha Nath V. Saroj Ranjan, AIR 1962 SC, 876. 

 5. Another wrong impression, though quite innocuous, requires to be dispelled before the principal question is gone into. The police, after investigating the case which was registered on the First Information Report, submitted a report calling it a Final Report under section 173 of the Criminal Procedure Code recommending that the accused persons shown therein should be 'discharged' or released from custody or from their bail bonds, as the case may be. But, in fact, there is no term like "Final report" or for that matter, "Charge-sheet" in section 173 of the Criminal P.C. Under this section, the Investigation Officer is required to submit on conclusion of an investigation a report which has been termed as a "police report". In that report the Investigation Officer shall either recommend that the accused persons should be prosecuted or that the accused should be "released". In the Police Regulations of Bengal a distinction has been made between these two kinds of recommendations for the sake of convenience and according to this distinction, the police-report containing recommendation for prosecution is called "Charge-sheet" and the police-report containing recommendation for discharging the accused is called Final Report. Both the Charge-sheet and the Final report constitute the police-report" under section. 173. The Magistrate, however, is not bowl to accept the recommendation made by the Investigating Officer in his report but he is required to apply his judicial discretion and he may disagree with the Investigating Officer. If the recommendation is that the accused should be discharged, in other words, if "Final-report" has been submitted, the Magistrate may, on rejecting the recommendation, adopt either of the two courses. If he finds from the statements of the witnesses record by the police that there are materials which warrant prosecution of the accused., the Magistrate may take cognizance of the offence on that Final-report and this cognizance must be treated as taken under clause (b) of section 190 (I) of the Cr.P.C. The cognizance taken thus will not be treated as one taken under clause (c) of section 190 (1) that is, it is not a cognizance taken on the Magistrate's own knowledge of information. I am supported in this view to the fullest extent by a decision of the Pakistan Supreme Court in the case of Falak Sher and others vs. State, 19 DLR (SC) 426. But this course is hardly adopted by a Magistrate obviously because, to proceed on this line requires painstaking examination of the police report including statements of the witnesses examined under section 161 of Cr.P.C. and also, in appropriate cases, the police diary itself. The Magistrate generally adopts the other course, which is rather easy, to direct the police to hold further investigation. And in case a Naraji-petition is filed either by the Informant or any other complainant, the Magistrate is free to take cognizance upon examination of the complainant, and, if necessary on examination of some witnesses, or by getting an enquiry held under section 202 by some other persons. Submission of 'Final Report' by the police therefore is not end of the whole matter. Acceptance of the 'Final-Report' necessarily results in the release of the accused from custody or from bail bond, as the case may be, and the Magistrate's Order releasing the accused is ordinarily referred to as an order of "discharge" although term "discharge" no-where appears in section 173. This 'discharge' must not be confused with 'discharge' under section 253 in the case of a Warrant Procedure under Chapter XXI, or under sec. 209 in the case of a committal proceeding under Chapter XVIII. "Discharge" there takes place after cognizance is taken and process is issued against a person. Both these Chapters have been altogether repealed by the recent Amendments of the Code of Criminal Procedure. But provision as to dismissal of a complaint under section 202 has remained unaltered. 'Dismissal' takes place where no cognizance is taken and no process is issued. But for the purpose of entertaining a fresh complaint ‘dismissal and 'discharge' are often placed on same footing. In a number of cases both before and after Partition of India, dismissal of a complaint under section 202 or discharge of an accused either under section 209 or 253 Cr.P.C. have been used in synonymous terms when the question arises whether a proceeding against the accused who have been discharged or in whose favour a complaint has been dismissed, can be revived. Again, a distinction t as been made between the same proceeding revived after 'dismissal' or 'discharge', and the enter attainment of a fresh complaint or fresh police report instead of revival of the previous proceedings. The distinction is in fact technical but still it is a distinction which cannot be ignored. In the case of 'revival' the question of the Magistrate becoming functus officio may arise, but no such question can arise if a fresh complaint is entertained though on the same allegation. This view has also been taken by the Pakistan Supreme Court in the case of Abdul Hossain Sana v. Swalal Agarwala, 14 DLR SC 96. 

 6. It is not disputed that after dismissal of a complaint or discharge of an accused, a fresh complaint may be entertained on the same allegation against the same person whether it is filed by the same complainant or by a different complainant but only in certain exceptional circumstances. Grounds for this principle are two: (1) dismissal of a complaint or discharge of an accused is not "acquittal" within the meaning of section 403 of the Criminal P.C. which expressly prohibits fresh prosecution of a person who has been acquitted ; (2) there is no provision in law that prohibits entertainment of a fresh  complaint after 'dismissal' or 'discharge'. Maclean, C.J. took this view in Queen Empress v. Dolegobind Das, 28 ILR Cal. 221 and Dwraka nath Mondal V Beni Madhab Banerjee ILR 28 Cal. 652 and observed that there is no basis for the contention that so long the order of dismissal or discharge remains unrevised fresh complaint cannot he entertained". Contrary view has also been expressed in many cases to the effect that when a complaint has been dismissed or the accused has been discharged on due consideration of all materials brought forward by the complainant, the Magistrate passing the order has exhausted all his power and he cannot revive the case Gr entertain a fresh complaint on the same allegation. Reasons given for this view are that there should be a finality of litigation and prosecution from harassment of the accused and that rimed against dismissible lies in revision by the Sessions Judge under section 436 or by the High Court under section 439, and that this power of revision will become redundant if the Magistrate revises his own order. Of those cases mention may be made of Nilratan Sett V. Queen Empress, 23 ILR Cal. 983 and Kamal Chandra Pal V. Queen Empress in ILA Cal. 286. In India, after Partition, these two inconsistent views were considered by the Supreme Court in the cases, Ram Gopal V., State of Bombay, AIR 1958 SC 97, Vadilal Panchal V. Dattatraya Dulaji, AIR 1960 SC 1113 and Pramatha Nath v. Saroj Ranjan, AIR 1962 SC 876, and it is in the last mentioned case that a harmonious interpretation of the relevant law has been given. In that case entertainment of a second complaint has been held to be "illegal and mere abuse of process of the Court" by majority of two of the three Judges; but it has been held to be perfectly lawful and "in the interest of justice" by the dissenting Judge. All the three learned Judges, however, are unanimous that there is no bar to entertainment of a second complaint 'in exceptional circumstances'; but they have differed on whether the 'exceptional circumstances' existed in that case. Mr. T.H. Khan argues that exceptional circumstances do not exist in the instant case also. As such, the views expressed there deserve careful consideration. 

 7. In the said Indian case, the first complaint was lodge in 1954 on she allegation that the accused persons, among other things, forged an "Agreement' by which Accused No. 1 was appointed Managing Director of a Private Limited Company, executed a false 'deed of transfer' in respect of certain shares of the Company and also forged the "Minute Book" . of the proceedings of meetings of the Board of Directors of the Company. The first complaint which had been filed on March 17, 1954 was dismissed and the dismissal was challenged before the High Court by a revisional application and thereafter before the Supreme Court by special leave. During the pendency of the appeal the complainant filed an application to withdraw the appeal on the ground that a compromise would be effected between the parties on the advice, of common friends and well-wishers, whereupon the appeal was dismissed and the order of 'dismissal' stood. After about a month, the complainant's brother however filed a fresh complaint on April 3, 1959 alleging that the compromise was brought about by undue influence and threat. This second complaint was entertained by the Chief Presidency Magistrate; a revisional application against the Magistrate's order was dismissed by the High Court whereupon the matter was brought to the Supreme Court again by an appeal. This appeal has been disposed of on the basis of the majority decision of two Judges who did not find any exceptional circumstances for entertaining the second complaint. 

 8. S.K. Das, J. who gave the dissenting judgment, however, found that the Presidency Magistrate who had dismissed the first complaint misdirected himself as to the scope and an effect of an enquiry under section 202 Cr. P.C. and misunderstood the provision, "sufficient ground for proceeding with the case" in that the Magistrate thought that sufficient grounds meant grounds sufficient to warrant an 'ultimate conviction'; secondly, the learned Judge found that an important fact which was not known to the complainant on the first occasion but which got a direct bearing on the allegation of forgery, was available when the second complaint was filed. It was that one of the alleged forged documents "Minute Book" of the Board's Meetings bore the date "16 January, 1948" and it was written on the official pad of the previous Managing Director, N.R. Sarkar, in which his Telephone number was stated to be "City Exchange 6091". It was, however, found from undisputed official record of the Telephone Directorate, that the City Exchange started functioning from December 1948; consequently, the Minute of the Board's meeting bearing the Telephone Exchange Number could not have been written on 16 January 1948 but was written after the City Exchange came into operation and the Minute was prima facie a forged document. The learned Judge further observed that the Magistrate did not keep in mind the true purpose of the enquiry before him which was only to as-certain whether there was evidence in support of the complaint so as to justify issue of process and commencement of the proceeding. The purpose of enquiry before the Magistrate, as further observed, was merely to ascertain prima facie the truth or falsehood of the complainant; instead of holding an enquiry into the complaint "the learned Chief Presidency Magistrate proceeded as though he was trying the case himself on merit". The learned Judge then concluded. 

 "I consider that this mistake on the part of the learned Chief Presidency Magistrate gave a wrong direction in the whole proceedings on the first complaint and the order of dismissal passed by him was due to a manifest error and resulted in miscarriage of justice." 

 9. But in the majority decision, it has been observed that the second complaint will be entertained "where the previous order was passed on an incomplete record or on a misunderstanding of the nature of the complaint or it was manifestly absurd, unjust or foolish or new fact which could not with reasonable diligence have been brought on the record in the previous proceeding, have been adduced. It cannot be said in the interest of justice that after the decision has been given against the complainant upon a full consideration of his case, he or any other person should be given another opportunity to have his complaint enquired." As to the fresh evidence that is, City Telephone Exchange 6091-coming into operation about one year after the relevant' date, the learned Judges did not accept the complainant's explanation that this fact was not known to him or his brother when the first complaint was filed and observed: 

 "It cannot be the law that the complainant may first place before the Magistrate some of the facts and evidence in his possession and if he fails he can then adduce some more evidence and so on." It appears that the second complaint in that case was finally dismissed by the Supreme Court in the facts and circumstances of that case only, particularly, in view of the fact that the previous case was withdrawn by the complainant from the Supreme Court. 

 10. The Pakistan Supreme Court in the case of Abul Hossain Sana as referred to above, has held that after discharge of the accused under section 253 of the Criminal P.C, a fresh prosecution on the same offence was illegal and gave the following reasons for this view: The complainant in that case could not produce any witnesses in spite of several adjournments having been given him whereupon the Magistrate found the allegation "groundless"; though the order of discharge is not "acquittal" within the meaning of section 403 Cr. P.C., but if the order of discharge was passed on consideration of all the evidence adduced by the prosecution which does not make out a prima facie case so as to frame a charge against the accused under section 254, then, the order of discharge amounts to an order of acquittal with the difference that in the case of 'acquittal' fresh prosecution is totally barred, and in the case of discharge, fresh prosecution is improper ; that though' there is no legal provision against the Magistrate taking fresh proceeding after discharge of the accused, he becomes functus officio since he has exhausted all his powers given under section 253 and is left with no more power to proceed against the accused on the same allegation: lastly, remedy against discharge has been provided in revision by the High Court or the Sessions Judge; this revisional power will become useless if the Magistrate himself revives his own order. In the instant case however the question centres round 'dismissal' which takes place before cognizance has been taken. In this case, the stage of discharge after cognizance has not yet come. The decision of the Pakistan Supreme Court has been referred to by the High Court Division so far it propounds the view that entertainment of a fresh proceeding, though on the same allegation, is different from revival of the same proceeding after discharge of the accused. 

 11. On consideration of the views in both Pakistan and Indian cases, we reaffirm the principle of law that a fresh complaint may be entertained after dismissal of the previous one or after acceptance of the 'Final Report', on the same allegation, against the same person; but this power of the Magistrate is not unqualified, unrestricted or unbridled. This power is circumscribed by so many factors which may collectively be termed as "exceptional circumstances". This power should be exercised very cautiously lest it frustrates the cause of justice by unnecessarily harassing a person complaint against whom has been dismissed or who has been released discharged on the basis of a police-report. This power should be exercised when the previous order of dismissal is manifestly illegal or absurd or when fresh materials come forward which were not available when the previous complaint was considered. Fresh complaint may also be entertained if the order of dismissal of the previous complaint had been passed on misunderstanding of the scope and extent of enquiry under sec. 202 Cr.P.C. In this case the police submitted Final-report on the ground that they did not find "any disinterested witnesses" to connect the accused with the incident resulting in the death of a person belonging to the complain ant’s party. It is not the case that there was no witness at all to implicate the accused, but it is a case of whether the witnesses who made statements to the police implicating the accused should be relied upon. This relates to weighing and assessment of evidence and credibility of witnesses a duty which is not of the Magistrate taking cognizance. This is the duty of the Court trying a case after cognizance has been taken. So, when the police recommended release of the accused on the ground that the witnesses were not disinterested the Magistrate should have ignored the recommendation simply on the ground that the assessment of evidence is not the duty of the Investigating Officer, as of himself  particularly when the offence alleged is exclusively triable by the Court of Session. Again, witnesses may not have made statements to the police implicating the accused, but if they depose before the Magistrate against the accused in an enquiry under section 202, the Magistrate cannot, unless it is absurd or foolish, reject the deposition on the ground of its being inconsistent with their statements to the police for, it is only during trial that assessment of such inconsistent evidence can be made. 

 12. Mr. T.H. Khan next contends that so far as these two appellants are concerned, they are highly respectable persons, one being Head Master of a High School and the other being Teacher of a Primary School, and that they were not at the scene of occurrence as the Investigating Officer himself found, but they were implicated out of political rivalry and personal enmity as they happened to be a Minister's relations. This is also a matter which can only be considered by the Court trying the accused the Magistrate taking cognizance on the basis of an enquiry under section 202 is not empowered to take this matter into consideration. At this stage his jurisdiction is limited to ascertaining the truth or otherwise of the allegation. In this case, the Magistrate passing the order of discharge 'misconceived' the extent of his power. Lastly, Mr. T.H. Khan contends that on repeal of the provision for committing the accused to the Court of Session for trial, the Magistrate's power has been reduced to the mere forwarding of the case-record to that Court, on receipt of a complaint or police report; consequently, the Magistrate's power of taking cognizance on a fresh complaint after dismissal of a previous one has been affected by necessary implication. We do not agree on this view, and we find that the Magistrate's power of taking cognizance under section 190(1) in all cases, including those exclusively triable by a Court of Session has remained unaffected by the repeal.
